hypotheses.title: notifyRewardAmount lacks REWARD_MANAGER_ROLE check
hypotheses.description: The function is declared `external nonReentrant whenNotPaused` with no role modifier, despite being the privileged reward-funding entry point. Any untrusted caller can invoke it for any whitelisted reward token, transferring their own tokens in and resetting the reward rate/periodFinish for all stakers. The NatSpec and role design (REWARD_MANAGER_ROLE) clearly intend this to be restricted, but the modifier is missing.
hypotheses.attackPath: 1) Attacker calls `notifyRewardAmount([whitelistedToken], [1])` with a tiny amount. 2) `_addRewardsForToken` recomputes `state.rate` and pushes `periodFinish` forward, diluting or resetting the ongoing reward schedule. 3) Attacker repeats at will to grief reward distribution and manipulate `perTokenStored`/`lastUpdated` accounting for all stakers.
hypotheses.impact: Reward schedule manipulation and griefing; existing stakers' pending rewards are diluted or their accrual window is reset, causing wrong accounting and potential loss of expected rewards.

hypotheses.title: __vesting_init is public and re-callable via SymmVesting
hypotheses.description: `__vesting_init` is declared `public initializer`, so it is externally callable. Although `initializer` prevents re-entry on the same proxy, the function is exposed on the implementation and on any derived contract that does not call it during its own initialization. If `SymmVesting.initialize` is front-run or if the implementation is used directly, an attacker can call `__vesting_init` to grant themselves all roles (DEFAULT_ADMIN, SETTER, PAUSER, UNPAUSER, OPERATOR) and set `lockedClaimPenalty`/`lockedClaimPenaltyReceiver`.
hypotheses.attackPath: 1) Attacker calls `__vesting_init(attacker, 0, attacker)` on an uninitialized proxy or implementation. 2) Attacker receives all roles. 3) Attacker uses SETTER_ROLE to set vesting plans and OPERATOR_ROLE to claim on behalf of users, or sets penalty to 100% to drain via `_claimLockedToken`.
hypotheses.impact: Full takeover of vesting logic; attacker can mint/claim tokens, set arbitrary vesting plans, and redirect penalties.
hypotheses.recommendation: Make `__vesting_init` `internal` (or `onlyInitializing`) so it can only be invoked from a derived contract's `initialize`.

hypotheses.title: getLiquidityQuote uses manipulable spot pool balances for USDC amount
hypotheses.description: getLiquidityQuote() derives the required USDC amount directly from POOL.getCurrentLiveBalances() (spot balances) with no TWAP or manipulation resistance. An attacker can flash-loan and swap against the pool to skew the SYMM/USDC balance ratio, inflating or deflating usdcAmount. The maxUsdcIn check is only a ceiling, so a manipulated quote that lowers usdcAmount lets the attacker pay less USDC while still receiving LP proportional to the manipulated ratio.
hypotheses.attackPath: 1) Attacker flash-borrows large USDC, swaps into the pool to push usdcBalance/symmBalance ratio down. 2) Calls addLiquidity with a large symmIn; getLiquidityQuote returns a small usdcAmount. 3) Router mints LP based on manipulated balances; attacker receives more LP than fair. 4) Attacker reverses the swap to restore pool, repays flash loan, keeps excess LP value.
hypotheses.impact: Attacker drains value from the pool/LP holders; vesting users adding liquidity get mispriced USDC requirements; protocol loses funds.
hypotheses.recommendation: Use a manipulation-resistant oracle (TWAP) or compute the quote from the router's actual proportional math with a post-trade balance check, and enforce a minimum LP per USDC spent.

hypotheses.title: initialize can be front-run to seize admin roles
hypotheses.description: `initialize` is `external initializer` with no access restriction and no check that the caller is the deployer. In a proxy deployment, if the implementation is deployed and the proxy is not initialized in the same transaction, any untrusted actor can call `initialize` first and grant themselves DEFAULT_ADMIN_ROLE, REWARD_MANAGER_ROLE, PAUSER_ROLE, and UNPAUSER_ROLE. The same pattern exists in `SymmVesting.initialize` and `Vesting.__vesting_init`.
hypotheses.attackPath: 1) Deployer deploys proxy pointing at implementation. 2) Before the intended `initialize` tx lands, attacker calls `initialize(attacker, stakingToken)` (or the vesting equivalent). 3) Attacker now holds all roles and can pause, unpause, configure reward tokens, claim for users, and rescue tokens.
hypotheses.impact: Full protocol takeover: attacker can pause/unpause, whitelist malicious reward tokens, drain via `rescueTokens`, and manipulate vesting plans.
hypotheses.recommendation: Use `initializer` plus an `onlyDeployer`/`_disableInitializers()` pattern on the implementation, or initialize atomically in the proxy constructor.

hypotheses.title: SymmVesting.initialize is public and front-runnable
hypotheses.description: `initialize` is `public initializer` with no caller restriction. If the proxy is deployed without atomic initialization, an untrusted actor can call it first, becoming admin and receiving all roles via `__vesting_init`, and setting POOL/ROUTER/PERMIT2/VAULT/SYMM/USDC/SYMM_LP to attacker-controlled addresses. This lets the attacker redirect all liquidity operations and token flows.
hypotheses.attackPath: 1) Attacker front-runs the intended `initialize` call. 2) Attacker passes malicious `_pool`, `_router`, `_permit2`, `_vault`, `_symm`, `_usdc`, `_symm_lp`. 3) Subsequent `addLiquidity` calls route user USDC/SYMM through attacker contracts.
hypotheses.impact: Theft of user USDC/SYMM during `addLiquidity`, full protocol takeover, and arbitrary role assignment.
hypotheses.recommendation: Initialize atomically in the proxy constructor or guard `initialize` with a deployer-only check plus `_disableInitializers()` on the implementation.

hypotheses.title: SymmVesting getLiquidityQuote decimals mismatch for USDC
hypotheses.description: `usdcAmount = (symmAmount * usdcBalance) / symmBalance` computes USDC in pool-native decimals (USDC has 6 decimals). Then `usdcAmount = _mulDivUp(usdcAmount, 1e18, 1e30)` multiplies by 1e18 and divides by 1e30, which is a net division by 1e12 — this converts 6-decimal USDC to 18-decimal USDC. However, `_addLiquidity` then uses `usdcIn` directly as the amount to `safeTransferFrom` from the user and to pass to the router. If the pool's USDC is 6-decimal, the router expects 6-decimal amounts, but `usdcIn` is now 18-decimal (1e12× too large). Conversely, if the intent was to normalize to 18 decimals for internal math, the value passed to the router is wrong.
hypotheses.attackPath: 1) User calls `addLiquidity` with a SYMM amount. 2) `getLiquidityQuote` returns `usdcIn` scaled by 1e12 relative to actual USDC needed. 3) `usdc.safeTransferFrom(msg.sender, address(this), usdcIn)` pulls 1e12× more USDC than required (or reverts if user lacks balance). 4) If user has balance, they lose 1e12× the intended USDC.
hypotheses.impact: Massive over-payment of USDC by the user; loss of funds.
hypotheses.recommendation: Remove the `_mulDivUp(usdcAmount, 1e18, 1e30)` scaling, or apply it only for internal 18-decimal math and convert back before transferring/approving.

hypotheses.title: _addLiquidity passes expectedLpAmount as minLpAmount to router, ignoring user slippage
hypotheses.description: The router call uses expectedLpAmount (the spot-derived quote) as the minimum LP argument, not the user-supplied minLpAmount or minLpAmountWithSlippage. The user's slippage protection is only checked after the router call via lpAmount < minLpAmountWithSlippage, but the router itself is allowed to mint as little as expectedLpAmount which equals the quote — meaning if the pool is manipulated between quote and execution, the router's internal min is the manipulated expected value, not the user's floor. Worse, when minLpAmount==0 the default is expectedLpAmount*99/100, still derived from the manipulable quote.
hypotheses.attackPath: 1) Attacker observes a victim's addLiquidity tx in mempool. 2) Front-runs by skewing pool balances so expectedLpAmount computed at execution is lower than fair. 3) Router accepts the low expectedLpAmount as min; victim receives fewer LP than the 1% default intends relative to fair value. 4) Attacker back-runs to profit.
hypotheses.impact: Victims receive less LP than intended; sandwich extraction of value from vesting users.
hypotheses.recommendation: Pass minLpAmountWithSlippage (the user's floor) as the router's minLpAmount argument, and derive the default from a manipulation-resistant source.

hypotheses.title: Reverting reward token blocks all deposits, withdrawals, and claims
hypotheses.description: `_updateRewardsStates` iterates over all entries in `rewardTokens` and calls `rewardPerToken(token)` for each. If any whitelisted reward token becomes blacklisting (e.g., USDC blacklists the staking contract), a malicious reward token is added by the reward manager, or the token is otherwise non-transferable/reverting, the loop reverts. Since deposit, withdraw, claimRewards, claimFor, notifyRewardAmount, and configureRewardToken all call `_updateRewardsStates(address(0))`, a single bad reward token freezes the entire contract for every user.
hypotheses.attackPath: 1. An attacker obtains the REWARD_MANAGER_ROLE (or is a malicious/compromised manager per attacker model where the role is granted in initialize to admin — the manager is a trusted role, so instead the untrusted path is a third-party reward token already whitelisted). 2. A whitelisted reward token is a malicious ERC20 whose `transfer`/`balanceOf` reverts (e.g., after the attacker becomes the token owner and toggles a revert flag). 3. Every call to `deposit`, `withdraw`, `claimRewards`, or `notifyRewardAmount` reverts inside the loop. 4. Users cannot unstake SYMM or claim rewards.
hypotheses.impact: All staked SYMM and pending rewards are permanently frozen for every user; withdrawals are impossible. Full loss of user access to funds.
hypotheses.recommendation: Skip reverting tokens (try/catch), or make the token iteration resilient, or ensure only vetted tokens can be whitelisted and provide a per-user escape that bypasses the full iteration.

hypotheses.title: SymmVesting._addLiquidity uses block.timestamp for Permit2 expiration, causing immediate expiry
hypotheses.description: The Permit2 approvals are set with `uint48(block.timestamp)` as the expiration. Permit2's `approve` function sets the allowance with the given expiration, and the router's `addLiquidityProportional` call will check the allowance. Since the expiration equals the current block timestamp, the allowance is considered expired at the moment of the call (Permit2 checks `block.timestamp <= expiration`). This causes the router call to revert, making `addLiquidity` and `addLiquidityByPercentage` unusable. The user's USDC is pulled before the revert, but the entire transaction reverts, so no funds are lost, but the function is effectively broken.
hypotheses.attackPath: 1. Any user calls `addLiquidity` or `addLiquidityByPercentage`. 2. The function pulls USDC from the user, approves Permit2 with expiration = block.timestamp. 3. The router call reverts because the allowance is expired. 4. The entire transaction reverts, so the user cannot add liquidity.
hypotheses.impact: Denial of service on the liquidity addition feature; users cannot add liquidity.
hypotheses.recommendation: Set the Permit2 expiration to `block.timestamp + 1` or a larger buffer, or use `type(uint48).max` for single-transaction approvals.

hypotheses.title: Reward rate dilution via repeated notifyRewardAmount with tiny amounts
hypotheses.description: When a reward period is ongoing, `_addRewardsForToken` computes `state.rate = (amount + leftover) / state.duration` and then resets `state.periodFinish = block.timestamp + state.duration`. Because `leftover = remaining * state.rate` is truncated integer math and the new `amount` is divided by the full `duration` (not the remaining time), a reward manager (or anyone with REWARD_MANAGER_ROLE) can repeatedly call notify with tiny amounts to extend the period and dilute the effective rate. More importantly, the `pendingRewards[token]` accounting is incremented by the full `amount` while the rate is recomputed against the full duration, so the sum of `rate * duration` can exceed the actual tokens deposited, causing the contract to promise more rewards than it holds.
hypotheses.attackPath: 1) Attacker (with REWARD_MANAGER_ROLE, or via a compromised manager) calls `notifyRewardAmount` with a very small amount (e.g., 1 wei) repeatedly. 2) Each call extends `periodFinish` by `duration` and recomputes `rate` using `(amount + leftover)/duration`, which under-counts the leftover because `leftover` is computed from the old rate over the remaining window but then divided by the full duration. 3) Over many calls, `rate * duration` grows beyond the total deposited, so `pendingRewards` is under-collateralized. 4) Stakers claim rewards that exceed the contract's balance, causing later claimers to revert or the contract to become insolvent.
hypotheses.impact: Insolvency of the reward pool; later stakers cannot claim; accounting mismatch between `pendingRewards` and actual token balance.
hypotheses.recommendation: Compute the new rate using the remaining duration for the leftover portion, or require that `amount + leftover` be divided by the remaining time, and cap `rate * duration` to the actual deposited amount.

hypotheses.title: SymmVesting assumes poolTokens[0]=SYMM and [1]=USDC without validation
hypotheses.description: The code retrieves `poolTokens = POOL.getTokens()` and blindly assigns `(IERC20 symm, IERC20 usdc) = (poolTokens[0], poolTokens[1])`. It then approves and transfers based on this assumption, and `getLiquidityQuote` similarly assumes `balances[0]` is SYMM and `balances[1]` is USDC. If the pool's token ordering differs (or is changed by the pool admin), the contract will approve/transfer the wrong tokens and compute wrong quotes, potentially sending USDC as if it were SYMM.
hypotheses.attackPath: 1) If the pool's token order is not [SYMM, USDC], a user calling `addLiquidity` will have the wrong token pulled/approved. 2) An attacker can exploit the mispriced quote to extract value (e.g., by providing a pool where balances[0] is a cheap token) or cause the contract to transfer the wrong asset.
hypotheses.impact: Loss of user funds (wrong token transferred), incorrect LP minting, potential insolvency of the vesting contract.
hypotheses.recommendation: Validate that `poolTokens[0] == SYMM` and `poolTokens[1] == USDC` (or resolve indices dynamically by matching addresses) before proceeding.

hypotheses.title: Reward double-counting when a token is re-whitelisted after removal
hypotheses.description: When a reward token is removed from the whitelist, its entry is popped from `rewardTokens` but `rewardState[token]`, `userRewardPerTokenPaid`, and `rewards` mappings are not cleared. If the token is later re-whitelisted, `rewardState[token].duration` is reset to `DEFAULT_REWARDS_DURATION` but `perTokenStored`, `lastUpdated`, and `periodFinish` retain stale values. `_updateRewardsStates` will then compute `rewardPerToken` using the stale `lastUpdated` and `periodFinish`, potentially minting a large `perTokenStored` jump that credits users with rewards for a period during which the token was not whitelisted, and `pendingRewards[token]` may be insufficient to cover the claims.
hypotheses.attackPath: 1) A reward token is whitelisted and accrues rewards. 2) Manager removes it (pendingRewards <= 10). 3) Users' `rewards[user][token]` and `userRewardPerTokenPaid` remain. 4) Manager re-whitelists the token. 5) On next `_updateRewardsStates`, `rewardPerToken` uses stale `lastUpdated`/`periodFinish` and credits users with rewards that were never funded, draining `pendingRewards` and reverting claims for others.
hypotheses.impact: Users can claim rewards that were never deposited; `pendingRewards[token]` underflows on claim, reverting and freezing all claims for that token.
hypotheses.recommendation: On removal, zero out `rewardState[token]`, `userRewardPerTokenPaid`, and `rewards` for that token, or snapshot and reset state on re-whitelist.

hypotheses.title: rescueTokens lets admin drain staking/reward tokens
hypotheses.description: `rescueTokens` is guarded only by `DEFAULT_ADMIN_ROLE` and transfers any token, including `stakingToken` and whitelisted reward tokens, to an arbitrary receiver. There is no exclusion for tokens backing user stakes or pending rewards, so the admin can withdraw funds that belong to stakers. While admin is a trusted role, the function's unrestricted scope means a compromised or malicious admin key can cause protocol insolvency.
hypotheses.attackPath: 1) Admin (or attacker who compromises the admin key) calls `rescueTokens(stakingToken, totalSupply, attacker)`. 2) All staked principal is transferred out. 3) Users' `withdraw` calls revert on insufficient balance.
hypotheses.impact: Complete loss of staked principal and pending reward tokens; protocol insolvency and frozen user funds.
hypotheses.recommendation: Restrict `rescueTokens` to non-staking, non-reward tokens, or track and exclude balances backing `totalSupply` and `pendingRewards`.

hypotheses.title: SymmStaking reward rate truncation causes stuck pendingRewards
hypotheses.description: When `notifyRewardAmount` is called, `pendingRewards[token]` is incremented by the full `amount`, but `state.rate` is set to `amount / state.duration` (integer division). The truncated remainder is never accounted for, so `pendingRewards[token]` will always exceed the sum of rewards actually distributable via `rate * duration`. Over time, `pendingRewards[token]` drifts upward relative to real claimable rewards, and `_claimRewardsFor` subtracts from `pendingRewards` only the actual claimed amounts, leaving a growing residual that can never be claimed but blocks `configureRewardToken(token, false)` (which reverts if `pendingRewards[token] > 10`).
hypotheses.attackPath: 1) Reward manager notifies a reward amount not evenly divisible by `duration` (e.g., 1 wei with 1 week duration → rate = 0). 2) `pendingRewards[token]` increases by 1 wei but no rewards are ever distributed. 3) Repeated small notifications accumulate residual `pendingRewards` that cannot be claimed. 4) Admin cannot delist the token because `pendingRewards[token] > 10` triggers `OngoingRewardPeriodForToken`. (Note: reward manager is trusted, but the drift is a code-level accounting bug reachable through normal operation.)
hypotheses.impact: Permanent accounting drift; reward tokens cannot be delisted; `pendingRewards` no longer reflects real obligations.
hypotheses.recommendation: Track the actual distributable amount (`rate * duration`) in `pendingRewards`, or accumulate the truncated remainder into the next period.

hypotheses.title: _addRewardsForToken rate truncation and leftover math can strand or misprice rewards
hypotheses.description: state.rate = amount / state.duration truncates; when block.timestamp < periodFinish, rate = (amount + leftover)/duration where leftover = remaining*rate uses the already-truncated rate, compounding rounding loss. Over many notify cycles the sum of rate*duration can be less than the deposited amount, leaving pendingRewards[token] permanently above what can be paid out, and _claimRewardsFor will underflow pendingRewards if accounting drifts. No minimum amount or precision scaling is enforced.
hypotheses.attackPath: An untrusted reward notifier (anyone can call notifyRewardAmount for whitelisted tokens) repeatedly notifies tiny amounts just after period start, forcing repeated truncation; accumulated dust becomes unclaimable and pendingRewards accounting diverges from actual distributable rewards, eventually causing claim reverts or stuck funds.
hypotheses.impact: Reward tokens stuck in contract; pendingRewards underflow reverts blocking claims; users receive less than notified.
hypotheses.recommendation: Scale rate by 1e18 (rate = amount*1e18/duration) and track distributed vs pending precisely, or reject amounts below duration to avoid truncation.
